newsitem.title: MALDIVES: S.Asian nations take hard look at cold facts.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian nations take hard look at cold facts.

text.p: South Asia's leaders spent three days soul-searching in a tropical paradise this week and decided their regional bloc needed to be revitalised to ease widespread deprivation plaguing many of its 1.2 billion people.
The leaders who attended the ninth South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) summit in the island nation of the Maldives were disarmingly candid about the bloc's shortcomings.

"Does the proliferation of activities over the last decade signify anything more than the growth of barren foliage on a vast tree? What fruit has SAARC truly borne?" Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga said.

Poverty, illiteracy and undernourishment -- the realities of the region -- were not lost on the leaders of the seven nations even if they were sheltered in a luxury resort surrounded by the emerald waters of the Indian Ocean.
"There are areas in which we have moved very slowly," Maldivian President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom told a news conference at the end of the summit on Wednesday.
Leader after leader spoke frankly about the region's burdensome problems and the pressing need to do more. It was unclear whether they would find the recipe for success.
"South Asia remains one of the world's poorest, most illiterate and malnourished regions," Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said.

"Its economies are poor, agrarian and vulnerable to outside shocks of all types," she said. "The pace of poverty reduction, particularly for the extremely poor, has been distressingly slow. Much more needs to be done."

The seven SAARC nations -- Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka -- have one fifth of the world's people. The annual per capita income of $309 is the lowest in the world and lags behind sub-Saharan Africa's $555.

There are more children out of school in South Asia than in the rest of the world, according to the Islamabad-based Human Development Centre. Some 337 million people in the region lack safe drinking water, and 400 million go hungry every day.
The stock-taking summit -- the first in two years -- took place against the backdrop of prolonged economic growth in East and South East Asia.

The Maldivian president said South Asia was dogged by inadequate education and pervasive poverty. "All these together make a lot of difference between this region and other regions of the world which are more progressive," he said.
Long accustomed to trade barriers and split by regional rivalries, SAARC leaders agreed it was time to turn a page.

"There can be no looking back on the wasted years of the past," Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif said. "We have to wake up from the slumber of inaction... We either join the global mainstream or become marginalised."
The Sri Lankan president said: "Our tangible achievement to date has been relatively insubstantial, especially in the core areas of economic interaction."
One of the central decisions was to advance a deadline for forming a free trade zone to 2001 from 2005. The leaders called for deeper tariff concessions in the next round of trade talks.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral said SAARC had to "ensure that what began as a trickle in the first round is converted into a cascade".
By far the biggest economy in the region, India said SAARC should set its sights on the eventual creation of a South Asian Economic Community (SAEC), modelled on the European Union.

SAEC would promote a regional investment regime, export-oriented joint ventures, easy movement of goods and capital, and scientific cooperation. But India's suggestion that a single currency should be considered drew lukewarm support.
In a repudiation of the past, the SAARC leaders said a ban on political dialogue at summits should be ended in the interests of overcoming the mistrust that held back cooperation.
"We cannot afford the continuation of tensions, military confrontations and escalating defence budgets," Sharif said. "We have to channel our energies to improve the quality of life for our peoples."
